title: Follow the Money: What Happens Between “Pay” and “Paid”

know: The four-party model (cardholder, issuer, acquirer, merchant, with the network between the two banks) and how three-party networks, bank-transfer schemes and wallets differ from it.
What processor, gateway, payment service provider, payment facilitator and platform mean, and which of them is a network member and holds money.
The six steps of the timeline (authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, payout, dispute window), with what moves at each: a message, a record or money.
believe: The provider that answers the API call reports other parties' decisions; it does not make the decisive ones.
can_do: For any step of a card payment, name the party that acts, what it promises and whether money has moved.
Ask of any provider, in any country, which legal entity is the acquirer for the payment.

audience.who: A software engineer or architect who is new to payments and has just been asked to integrate, operate or evaluate a payment provider.
already_knows: APIs, webhooks, retries, queues and databases.
From the preface: that the instant answer is not the truth, the sixteen failure patterns, Larkfield and Mila's €120 class pass.
From the part introduction: that a payment is a chain of promises, and the €120 that came back three weeks after it succeeded.
does_not_know: Issuer, acquirer, card network, processor, gateway, payment service provider, payment facilitator.
Authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, payout, dispute, interchange.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a card payment the chapter does not contain, the reader names the parties in the order they act and says which of them holds the money at a stated moment.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer in Lyon pays €60 by card in a bakery's ordering app at 08:10. At 08:11, who has decided what, who holds the €60, and which parties have not yet done anything?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The customer's bank (the issuer) has approved and holds the money, now reserved on the customer's account; the card network carried the request and the bakery's acquirer or provider relayed it; no money has moved; clearing, settlement between the banks and the payout to the bakery are still to come, and the customer can dispute for months.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every term the rest of the book relies on from this chapter (issuer, acquirer, network, provider, payment facilitator, authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, payout, dispute) is defined in one plain clause before it is used.

Every statement about which role Stripe or Adyen plays is a dated, sourced fact or is marked as not public; the table of who holds money and risk is labeled as a generalization that contracts and local law can change.

thesis.question: What has to happen, between which parties, for one card payment to be approved, collected, moved, paid out and possibly taken back?
thesis.claim: One card payment takes six steps spread over days and carried out by at least five parties (the acquirer and the provider may be one company): the issuer approves, the merchant captures, the acquirer presents a clearing record through the network, the network nets what its member banks owe each other, the provider pays the merchant, and for about 120 days the cardholder can have it taken back. The provider that answers the API call controls none of the three steps that decide the outcome: it does not make the approval decision, does not run the settlement between banks and cannot stop a dispute.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a payment is a transaction between the merchant and its payment provider, in which the provider takes the money and the other parties are details the API rightly hides.
thesis.so_what: If the provider only relays and records other parties' promises, then its status fields are reports with a delay, and an integrator must ask of each one whose decision it reports and what is still open; the first question to put to any provider becomes which entity is the acquirer for this payment in this country.
thesis.how_why: The annual reports Visa and Mastercard published in 2026 describe the same four-party structure and say the networks neither issue cards nor hold customers' money; they route the authorization, exchange clearing records and settle between members. A provider packages the acquirer's side of that structure, and which role it plays is a per-country fact. Stripe's acquirer disclosure (n.d., accessed November 2026) names Stripe entities as acquirer in Europe and six acquirers in the United States (five banks and Stripe's own limited-purpose bank), where Stripe acts as a payment facilitator; Adyen holds a banking license from the Dutch central bank and lists the countries and regions where it has an acquiring connection and names the acquiring entity for some markets only. Neither publishes an end-to-end description of its own role by region.

supporting_claims.claim: A card payment has at least five parties, and the roles that matter (issuer, acquirer, network) are defined by membership and license, not by technology; other payment methods merge or remove some of them.
The payment is six steps on separate clocks in which first a message, then a record and only then money moves, so the approval the customer sees moves nothing.

The approval, the settlement between banks and the dispute each belong to a party other than the provider, which can only relay and record them, so its statuses are delayed reports and each hand-off can fail on its own.
Which role a provider plays is a per-country fact: Stripe publishes its acquirer per country, Adyen publishes its licenses but no such list, and neither describes its role end to end.

role.contribution: Supplies the parties, the six-step timeline and the distinction between messages and money that every later chapter places itself on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: timeline and in-practice: the six steps in the order they happen
scene to in-practice: the studio owner's question is posed in the first section and answered in the seventh

flow.rationale: Each section supplies the terms the next one uses. The scene poses four questions; the parties section names who answers them; the timeline puts those parties in order, which it could not do before they were defined; the variants section needs both the parties and the steps to say what other methods remove; the provider's positions are stated in terms of settlement and payout, so they follow the timeline; the Stripe and Adyen table fills in those positions; Mila's payment then uses everything at once, and the failures are read off the same six steps. Put the timeline before the parties and each step would name actors the reader has not met; put the company comparison before the positions and its rows (payment facilitator, acquirer of record) would be undefined; put Mila's walkthrough first and it would be a list of unexplained names.

hook.content: At 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027 Mila Janssen buys a ten-class pass for €120.00 in the Larkfield app and two seconds later the screen says the payment succeeded. At 19:43, where is the €120? Still in her own bank account.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer sees a payment as a request that returned success, and stores that as the payment's status.
bridge.to_topic: The success was one bank's promise; five more steps, carried out by parties the API hides, decide whether the merchant ever keeps the money.

thesis_statement.text: One card payment takes six steps spread over days and carried out by at least five parties, and the provider that answers the API call controls none of the three steps that decide the outcome: the approval, the settlement between banks and the dispute.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout, first bullet, and paragraph p02

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p05

promises.promise: Start from a studio owner's question at Larkfield about a payment marked 'paid', and answer it with Mila's €120 followed party by party.
Define the parties of the four-party model and the trade names layered on it, with who holds the money and the risk.
Lay out the six-step timeline and what moves at each step: a message, a record or money.
Show how three-party networks, bank transfers and wallets depart from the model.
Describe the positions a provider can take in the chain, and what Stripe and Adyen each document about their own.
Show how each step fails and the rule for detecting it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At 19:42 Mila's app says the €120 payment succeeded, and a minute later the €120 is still in her own bank account: only a message has moved.

evidence.what: Mila's class pass: Tuesday 9 March 2027, 19:42, a ten-class pass for €120.00 at Studio Noord, paid with a Dutch Visa debit card from her phone's wallet; Larkfield introduced as fictional.
evidence.shows: The gap between the answer on the screen and the place the money is, in a case with exact time and amount.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One card payment takes six steps over days and at least five parties, and the provider that answers the API call controls none of the three steps that decide the outcome: the approval, the settlement between banks and the dispute.

transition_in.carries_over: The puzzle of a success message with no money moved.
transition_in.introduces: The explanation: the answer was the issuer's promise, the first of six steps carried out by different parties.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the provider only relays and records other parties' promises, every status it returns is a report with a delay, and the integrator has to ask of each one whose decision it reports and what is still open.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'Payment methods', https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "A `succeeded` status indicates that the payment completed successfully according to the payment method's processing flow, but funds can still be refunded, disputed, returned, or reversed".
evidence.shows: A provider says in its own documentation that its success status is not the end of the payment.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that the provider controls none of the deciding steps.
transition_in.introduces: What that means for anyone who stores or acts on a provider's status.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: This chapter covers the whole of Mila's class pass at low resolution, from 19:42 on Tuesday to the studio's payout on Thursday and the dispute window after it; every later chapter enlarges one stretch of it.

evidence.what: Mila's class pass: approved 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, captured automatically, in the studio's payout on Thursday 11 March.
evidence.shows: Places the chapter on the recurring payment's path.

transition_in.carries_over: The six steps as an abstract claim.
transition_in.introduces: The one payment the book follows through them, and how much of it this chapter covers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter goes from a scene at Larkfield to the parties, the timeline, the payment methods that bend the model, the places a provider can stand, the Stripe and Adyen comparison, Mila's payment party by party, and the ways each step fails.

transition_in.carries_over: The payment the chapter follows.
transition_in.introduces: The order of the chapter's sections.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: One Word for Four Facts
sections.controlling_idea: A studio owner asks where her €120 is while Larkfield's record says 'paid', and the one word turns out to stand for four different facts that four different parties hold.

advances_thesis.how: Shows, before any vocabulary, a status that is true and still does not answer whether money has moved or can come back.

flow.rationale: The owner's question first, then the four questions it breaks into; the reader meets the problem as a support ticket before it is named.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's claim that a status is a delayed report of someone else's promise.
transition_in.introduces: The morning after Mila's payment, when a studio owner reads the status as money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Wednesday 10 March 2027 Ines Bakker sees Mila's pass marked 'paid' in the Larkfield back office, finds no €120 in Studio Noord's bank account and asks support where it is.

evidence.what: Ines Bakker, owner of Studio Noord; Aylin Demir, Head of Studio Support; the payment record store's five-state vocabulary (pending, authorized, paid, refunded, disputed). The ticket on 10 March is a local detail consistent with the ledger's payout date of 11 March.
evidence.shows: A reasonable person reads 'paid' as 'I have the money', and the record gives her no way to know otherwise.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke de Graaf answers with four questions the word 'paid' cannot answer (who approved, has any money moved, when does the studio receive it, until when can it be taken back), each of which has a different party behind it.

evidence.what: The four questions map to the issuer, the network's settlement, the provider's payout and the cardholder's dispute right.
evidence.shows: The single status hides four facts with four owners, which is the chapter's question in miniature.

evidence.what: Conceptual figure: one green tick on a phone beside a chain of four promise notes, each with its own clock (placeholder 01-one-tick-four-promises).
evidence.shows: Makes the central point memorable: one visible answer, several open promises.

transition_in.carries_over: Ines's reading of 'paid' as money received.
transition_in.introduces: The four separate facts the word stands for.

sections.heading: The Parties: Four in the Model, More in Practice
sections.controlling_idea: The card networks define four parties with the network between the two banks, the roles that matter are defined by membership and license and not by technology, and the trade names layered on top (processor, gateway, provider, payment facilitator, platform) differ in whether they are network members and whether they hold money.

advances_thesis.how: Names the at-least-five parties and says which of them holds money and which carries risk.

flow.rationale: The four parties first, then the network that connects them, then the acquirer defined against the network, then the trade names defined against the acquirer, then money and risk for all of them. Each definition uses only the ones before it; the money-and-risk table cannot come first because its rows are the parties.

transition_in.carries_over: The four questions, each with a different party behind it.
transition_in.introduces: Who those parties are, in the card networks' own words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four-party model has a cardholder and the bank that issued the card (the issuer) on one side, a merchant and the institution that accepts cards for it (the acquirer) on the other, and the card network between the two institutions.

evidence.what: Visa 10-K: Visa provides "transaction processing services (primarily authorization, clearing and settlement) among consumers, issuing and acquiring financial institutions and sellers in a structure we call the “four-party” model".
evidence.shows: The network itself uses the term and names the parties.
evidence.source: Visa Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316126000134/v-20260930.htm, filed 2026-11-05

evidence.what: Mastercard 10-K: "account holder (a person or entity who holds a card or uses another device enabled for payment), issuer (the account holder’s financial institution), merchant and acquirer (the merchant’s financial institution)".
evidence.shows: The second large network describes the same structure, so it is the field's model and not one company's.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The network is not a bank: it issues no cards and holds no customer money, and what it does is carry the messages between issuer and acquirer and work out what they owe each other.

evidence.what: Visa 10-K: "Visa is not a financial institution. We do not issue cards, extend credit or set rates and fees for account holders of Visa card products nor do we earn revenue from or bear credit risk with respect to any of these activities."
evidence.shows: The party whose brand is on the card neither decides the approval nor holds the money.
evidence.source: Visa Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316126000134/v-20260930.htm, filed 2026-11-05

evidence.what: Mastercard 10-K: "We do not issue cards, extend credit, determine or receive revenue from interest rates or other fees charged to account holders by issuers".
evidence.shows: Same position at the other network.

transition_in.carries_over: The network as the fifth element between the two banks.
transition_in.introduces: What the network is and is not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An acquirer is defined by what it is allowed to do, not by its software: it is a member of the network that signs the merchant, submits its transactions and receives the settlement money, and it needs a regulator's license as well.

evidence.what: Visa Core Rules glossary: an Acquirer is "A Member that signs a Merchant or Payment Facilitator, provides a Cash Disbursement to a Cardholder, or loads funds to a Prepaid Card, and directly or indirectly enters a Transaction into Interchange".
evidence.shows: Acquiring is a membership role; 'directly or indirectly' allows someone else to run the connection.
evidence.source: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf, edition of 2026-10-24

evidence.what: Stripe Services Agreement, services terms, https://stripe.com/en-us/legal/ssa-services-terms, n.d., accessed 2026-11: a Payment Method Acquirer is authorized to "sponsor or submit Transactions at the request of merchants to the Payment Method Provider for authorization and clearing" and to "receive and remit settlement funds for authorized and cleared Transactions".
evidence.shows: The same role from a provider's contract: the acquirer submits for the merchant and receives the money.

evidence.what: Adyen knowledge hub, 'Acquiring bank', https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/acquiring-bank, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "Acquirers must be licensed by local financial regulators and card schemes to relay transactions."
evidence.shows: Two separate permissions: the regulator's and the network's.

transition_in.carries_over: The network and its members.
transition_in.introduces: The member on the merchant's side, defined precisely.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five trade names sit on top of the model, and the useful way to tell them apart is two questions: is it a network member, and does it hold the merchant's money.

evidence.what: Role / what it does / network member? / holds the merchant's money?, rows: acquirer, processor, gateway, payment facilitator, payment service provider, platform. Labeled as industry usage except the quoted Visa definitions.
evidence.shows: The names are commercial; membership and custody are the facts that distinguish them.

evidence.what: Visa Core Rules glossary: an Acquirer Processor is "A non-Member agent or processor that a Member has engaged"; a Payment Facilitator is "An entity that contracts with an Acquirer to deposit Transactions, receive settlement from, or contract with an Acquirer on behalf of a Sponsored Merchant".
evidence.shows: Two of the trade names have rule definitions, and both place the role under a member.
evidence.source: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf, edition of 2026-10-24

transition_in.carries_over: The acquirer as a defined, licensed role.
transition_in.introduces: The commercial names that are not defined that way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each party holds the money at a different moment and carries a different risk, and the network's guarantee covers the two institutions but stops before the merchant.

evidence.what: Party / holds the money when / carries which risk, seven rows from cardholder to platform; labeled as a generalization that contracts and local law can change.
evidence.shows: No single party holds the money or the risk for the whole payment.

evidence.what: Mastercard 10-K: "We guarantee the settlement of many of the transactions from issuers to acquirers ... We do not, however, guarantee payments to merchants by their acquirers".
evidence.shows: The merchant's exposure between settlement and payout is to its acquirer or provider, not to the network.

evidence.what: Structural figure: the four-party model with the network between the issuer and the acquirer, the provider beside the acquirer and the platform beside the merchant (placeholder 01-four-party-model).
evidence.shows: Where each party sits before the timeline sets them in motion.

transition_in.carries_over: The parties and their names.
transition_in.introduces: What each of them holds and risks.

sections.heading: The Timeline: A Message, a Record, Then Money
sections.controlling_idea: The payment is six steps on separate clocks, and what moves changes along the way: a message at authorization, a record at clearing, money only at settlement and payout, with the dispute window open after all of them.

advances_thesis.how: Lays out the six steps with the party that acts in each, and shows that the approval, the interbank settlement and the dispute belong to parties other than the provider.

flow.rationale: The steps in the order they happen, after one paragraph that names the three kinds of movement and one table that shows all six at once. Taking payout before settlement, or the dispute before payout, would describe money going back that has not yet arrived. The requirements table comes last because it asks what a record must hold for steps the reader has just met.

transition_in.carries_over: The parties, and what each holds and risks.
transition_in.introduces: The order in which they act and what moves at each step.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three different things move in a card payment (a message, a record and money), in that order, and the network offers them as three separate services.

evidence.what: Mastercard 10-K: "we enable the routing of a transaction to the issuer for its approval, facilitate the exchange of financial transaction information between issuer and acquirer after a successfully conducted transaction, and settle the transaction by facilitating the exchange of funds between parties via settlement banks chosen by us and our customers".
evidence.shows: Authorization, clearing and settlement in one sentence by a network: approval, then information, then funds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The six steps are authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, payout and the dispute window, each with its own actor, its own clock and its own promise.

evidence.what: Step / typical time after 'pay' / who acts / what moves / the promise made. Six rows. The time column is labeled as typical industry practice, not a rule.
evidence.shows: The whole timeline on one page, with the kind of movement per step.

evidence.what: Structural figure: six stations on a line from 'Pay' to the dispute window, grouped under message, record and money (placeholder 01-six-step-timeline).
evidence.shows: The same table as a picture the later chapters can point back to.

transition_in.carries_over: Three kinds of movement.
transition_in.introduces: The six steps they are spread over.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Authorization is the issuer's promise and capture is the merchant's claim on it; a hold appears on the cardholder's account, and no money moves in either step.

evidence.what: Visa 10-K: the acquirer presents the transaction data to Visa, "which in turn sends the transaction data to the issuer to check the account holder’s account balance or credit line for authorization".
evidence.shows: The decision is the issuer's; the network and acquirer carry it.
evidence.source: Visa Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316126000134/v-20260930.htm, filed 2026-11-05

evidence.what: Visa Core Rules, section 5.7.3.5, Table 5-11: a cardholder-initiated transaction in a card-absent environment has a maximum processing timeframe of 10 calendar days from a valid authorization.
evidence.shows: The promise has an expiry set by the network, not by the provider.
evidence.source: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf, edition of 2026-10-24

evidence.what: Adyen documentation, 'Capture', https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/capture.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "By default, payments are captured automatically without a delay, immediately after authorization of the payment request."
evidence.shows: Why most integrators never notice capture as a separate step.

transition_in.carries_over: The table of six steps.
transition_in.introduces: The first two, which move no money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Clearing sends the final record of the transaction from the acquirer to the issuer through the network, and settlement moves money for the first time, as one net amount per member per day.

evidence.what: Visa Core Rules glossary: a Presentment is "A Clearing Record that an Acquirer presents to an Issuer through Interchange"; Settlement is "The reporting and funds transfer of Settlement Amounts owed by one Member to another, or to Visa, as a result of Clearing"; a Settlement Amount is "The daily net amounts expressed in a Member’s Settlement Currency resulting from Clearing".
evidence.shows: Clearing is records, settlement is funds, and the funds are net and daily, not per transaction.
evidence.source: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf, edition of 2026-10-24

evidence.what: Visa 10-K: "the issuer posts the transaction to the consumer’s account and effectively pays the acquirer an amount equal to the value of the transaction, minus the interchange reimbursement fee (IRF)".
evidence.shows: The money that reaches the acquirer is already less than the sale.
evidence.source: Visa Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316126000134/v-20260930.htm, filed 2026-11-05

transition_in.carries_over: The promise and the claim.
transition_in.introduces: The record and the first movement of money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Payout is the provider's own step after network settlement, on a schedule the provider sets, and both providers use the word 'settlement' for it, so 'settled' names a different event at each layer.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'Payouts', https://docs.stripe.com/payouts.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "Stripe uses “T” to refer to the transaction time, which indicates the time of the original payment confirmation or capture", whereas "Some payment processors might start “T” from their internal settlement time, meaning when the funds land in their bank accounts."
evidence.shows: Stripe's 'settlement timing' counts from capture, not from the network's settlement.

evidence.what: Adyen documentation, 'Sales day payout', https://docs.adyen.com/account/sales-day-payout.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "the funds you get do not depend on the settlement timelines of the schemes and payment methods used by your shoppers"; Sales Day Payout Terms of Service, https://www.adyen.com/legal/sales-day-payout-terms-of-service, last update 2024-06-17: payout is initiated "irrespective of whether the funds are actually received by Adyen from the Acquirer or Scheme Owner".
evidence.shows: Adyen's payout day is likewise the provider's decision and can precede the money's arrival at Adyen.

transition_in.carries_over: Money arriving at the acquirer.
transition_in.introduces: Money leaving the provider for the merchant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The cardholder's right to dispute runs for about 120 days and so outlasts authorization, settlement and payout: the payment can be taken back after the merchant has been paid.

evidence.what: Visa Core Rules, chapter 11 dispute time-limit tables: an issuer may initiate a dispute within "120 calendar days from the Transaction Processing Date" for most dispute conditions (75 for the authorization conditions).
evidence.shows: The primary rule behind 'about 120 days'.
evidence.source: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, https://usa.visa.com/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf, edition of 2026-10-24

evidence.what: Adyen documentation, 'Dispute timeframes', https://docs.adyen.com/risk-management/understanding-disputes/dispute-timeframes.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "In general, a cardholder has a maximum of 120 calendar days from the transaction date to dispute a transaction"; "In some cases for Visa and Mastercard, the cardholder has a maximum of 540 calendar days".
evidence.shows: A provider's statement of the same window for Visa and Mastercard, with the longer outer limit; the Mastercard figure is reported through Adyen.

transition_in.carries_over: The forward steps, which end at payout.
transition_in.introduces: The one step that runs backward and stays open longest.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For each step the integrator's own record should hold a different fact, learn it from a different source and tolerate a different delay, which is the author's reading of the timeline as requirements.

evidence.what: Step / what your record should hold / how you learn it / how late it can be / if the message is lost. Six rows; delays marked as assumptions; labeled as the author's judgement.
evidence.shows: Turns the timeline into what a payment record needs, and previews why later parts exist.

transition_in.carries_over: Six steps with six owners and clocks.
transition_in.introduces: What that requires of the record an integrator keeps.

sections.heading: When the Model Bends: Three-Party Networks, Bank Transfers and Wallets
sections.controlling_idea: Other payment methods change the parties, the steps or the finality: a three-party network merges issuer and acquirer, a bank-transfer scheme has no card network and its own rules on taking money back, and a wallet is either a card payment with a different credential or a network of its own.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the party model against the methods that depart from it, so the reader knows which parts are general and which belong to four-party cards.

flow.rationale: Three departures from the model, ordered from the smallest change (two roles merged) to the largest (no card network), ending with wallets because Mila's own payment is one and it leads back to the card model.

transition_in.carries_over: The four-party parties and the six-step timeline.
transition_in.introduces: Payment methods in which some of those parties or steps are missing or merged.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In a three-party network one company is both issuer and acquirer, so the two banks and the network between them collapse into one party.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2015/751, recital 28, http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32015R0751, published 2015-05-19 (evidence age 11 years; in force): "‘three party payment card schemes’ (cardholder — acquiring and issuing scheme — merchant) and ‘four party payment card schemes’ (cardholder — issuing bank — acquiring bank — merchant)"; Article 2(18): a three-party scheme that licenses other providers to issue or acquire "is considered to be a four party payment card scheme".
evidence.shows: A legal definition of both models, and of when the first becomes the second.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'How disputes work', https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/how-disputes-work.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: a card network "might be an intermediary in front of an issuing bank as with Visa or Mastercard, or a standalone entity as with American Express".
evidence.shows: A provider names the classic example.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A bank-transfer scheme has no card network and often no authorization-then-capture, and whether the payer can take the money back is set by the scheme: never for iDEAL, for eight weeks without a reason for SEPA Direct Debit.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'iDEAL | Wero payments', https://docs.stripe.com/payments/ideal.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "Customers can’t dispute iDEAL | Wero payments with their bank."
evidence.shows: A method with no dispute window at all.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'SEPA Direct Debit payments', https://docs.stripe.com/payments/sepa-debit.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: customers can dispute "without providing a reason for up to 8 weeks after the debit"; Adyen documentation, https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/sepa-direct-debit.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "Eight weeks to dispute a SEPA payment without providing a reason."
evidence.shows: A method where the payer's right is stronger than a card dispute, stated the same way by both providers.

evidence.what: Larkfield's 2026 online mix: cards 52%, SEPA Direct Debit 21%, iDEAL 14%.
evidence.shows: Nearly half of Larkfield's online volume does not follow the card model.

transition_in.carries_over: A card network with two roles merged.
transition_in.introduces: Payment methods with no card network.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A wallet is one of two things: a carrier for a card credential, in which case the payment is still a four-party card payment, or an account with its own balance and its own rules.

evidence.what: Stripe documentation, 'Wallets', https://docs.stripe.com/payments/wallets.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: wallets let customers pay using "A saved payment credential (a tokenized card or bank account stored in the wallet)" or "A stored wallet balance (funds held in an account with the wallet provider)".
evidence.shows: The two kinds, in a provider's words.

evidence.what: Adyen documentation, 'Apple Pay', https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/apple-pay.md, n.d., accessed 2026-11: "Apple Pay uses network tokenization" and "supports liability shift for American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard, and Visa cards".
evidence.shows: The first kind runs on the card networks, so issuer, acquirer and dispute rights remain.

evidence.what: Mila pays from her phone's wallet with her Dutch Visa debit card; the wallet authenticates her on the device and there is no 3-D Secure challenge.
evidence.shows: The book's recurring payment is a wallet payment and still a four-party card payment.

transition_in.carries_over: Methods that leave the card networks.
transition_in.introduces: A method that looks different at checkout and may not leave them at all.

sections.heading: Where a Provider Can Stand in the Chain
sections.controlling_idea: A payment provider can be a gateway in front of someone else's acquirer, a payment facilitator under an acquiring bank, or the acquirer itself, the answer can differ by country for one provider, and a platform adds one more layer above any of them.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that 'the provider' is not one role, which is why the acquirer of record has to be asked for per country.

flow.rationale: The three positions and their trade-offs first, then the confusion to avoid (a direct connection is not acquiring), then the layer the book's example adds. The platform comes last because it sits on top of whichever position the provider takes.

transition_in.carries_over: The provider, so far placed loosely beside the acquirer.
transition_in.introduces: The three positions it can actually occupy and what each means for the merchant's money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: There are three positions, and they differ in who is the network member, who holds the merchant's funds between settlement and payout, and how many parties stand between the merchant and the network.

evidence.what: Position (gateway only / payment facilitator under an acquiring bank / acquirer itself) by: network member, who holds funds before payout, parties between merchant and network, when it fits. Labeled as industry usage and the author's judgement. The facilitator row quotes Visa Core Rules, section 5.3.1.2, edition of 2026-10-24: the acquirer is 'liable for all acts, omissions, and other adverse conditions caused by the Payment Facilitator and its Sponsored Merchants'.
evidence.shows: The trade-off table: each position moves the membership, the custody and the number of hops.

evidence.what: Structural figure: three lanes from merchant to network showing the gateway, facilitator and acquirer positions (placeholder 01-provider-positions).
evidence.shows: The three positions side by side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A direct technical connection to a card network is not the same as being the acquirer of record, and Stripe's own publications show both at once for the United States.

evidence.what: Stripe newsroom, https://stripe.com/en-ca/newsroom/news/direct-platform, published 2020-04-23 (evidence age 6.5 years): Stripe "now processes card transactions through direct integrations with all six major card networks in North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia Pacific".
evidence.shows: A claim about message connectivity.

evidence.what: Stripe acquirer disclosure: "Stripe, LLC is a Payment Facilitator of the following Payment Method Acquirers", listing Cross River Bank, Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, Fifth Third Bank, Pathward N.A., PNC Bank, N.A. and Stripe MALPB.
evidence.shows: A statement about who holds the membership in the same region: named banks, and one Stripe-owned limited-purpose bank.
evidence.source: Stripe, Acquirer Disclosure & Acquirer Terms, https://stripe.com/en-us/legal/acquirer-disclosure, n.d., accessed 2026-11

transition_in.carries_over: Positions defined by membership.
transition_in.introduces: A claim about connectivity that is easily mistaken for one about membership.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform such as Larkfield adds a layer above the provider without becoming a party to the money: the studio is the seller, the provider holds the studio's funds, and the platform takes a fee, so the first question about any provider is which legal entity acquires for these sellers in this country.

evidence.what: Larkfield never holds member funds; on both providers the studio's money sits in the provider's regulated balance until payout; Larkfield is not the merchant of record, the studio is the seller.
evidence.shows: The running example occupies the platform layer and deliberately not the money-holding one.

transition_in.carries_over: The provider's three positions.
transition_in.introduces: The platform layer on top, and the question that follows from all of it.

sections.heading: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ
sections.controlling_idea: Both companies are regulated institutions that acquire in their own name in Europe; they differ in the kind of license, in whether they publish who the acquirer is per country, and in the details of a payout clock that is the provider's own at both, and neither publishes an end-to-end account of its role by region.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the documented, dated answer to 'which role does the provider play' for the two anchor companies, and marks what is not public.

flow.rationale: The table of documented facts, then what an integrator does with it, then where the public record ends. The limits come last so the reader does not take the table for the whole picture.

transition_in.carries_over: The three positions a provider can take.
transition_in.introduces: Which positions Stripe and Adyen document for themselves, and where.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side from their own legal pages and documentation, the two companies differ in five aspects of where they stand in the chain.

evidence.what: Aspect / Stripe / Adyen / what the difference suggests. Rows: regulated form in the EEA (Stripe Technology Europe Limited, e-money institution authorized by the Central Bank of Ireland, https://stripe.com/stel/legal, published 2019-04-05, evidence age 7 years; Adyen N.V., credit institution under De Nederlandsche Bank, https://www.adyen.com/licenses/emea, n.d., accessed 2026-11); acquirer of record for an EEA card payment (Stripe disclosure names Stripe Technology Europe, Ltd.; Adyen's license page says the license includes cross-border acquiring in all EEA countries, no per-country acquirer list); role in the United States (Stripe, LLC a payment facilitator of five named banks and Stripe MALPB; Adyen N.V. San Francisco Branch licensed by the OCC and the Federal Reserve Board, https://www.adyen.com/licenses/united-states, n.d., accessed 2026-11); where own acquiring stops (Stripe publishes it per country; Adyen reports 84% of 2025 processed volume as full-stack and banking partners 'in locations where there are no own direct acquiring licenses', Annual Report 2025, signed 2026-03-05, https://investors.adyen.com/financials/2025); what the payout clock counts from (Stripe: capture, 3 business days default for the Netherlands after an initial 7 calendar days; Adyen: the sales day, typically 2 business days).
evidence.shows: Every cell is a dated company statement or 'Not public'; the last column is the author's inference.
evidence.source: Stripe, Acquirer Disclosure & Acquirer Terms, https://stripe.com/en-us/legal/acquirer-disclosure, n.d., accessed 2026-11

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Stripe an integrator can read the acquirer per country from a public page and should store it; on Adyen the same question has to be put to the account team for each market, and on both the payout day must not be read as the day the network settled.

transition_in.carries_over: The five documented differences.
transition_in.introduces: What an integrator does differently on each provider because of them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The public record stops at three points: a list of network memberships by network and country, the share of volume that runs through each acquirer, and a general statement of whether payouts wait for network settlement.

evidence.what: Stripe names five US partner banks and its own limited-purpose bank without shares; Adyen reports 84% full-stack volume without naming the acquirers of the rest; Adyen's Sales Day Payout terms say payout does not wait for funds, and Stripe's payout page does not say either way. An INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED block gives the author's reading of why one publishes a list and the other does not.
evidence.shows: Marks the boundary between documented fact and inference, as the book's evidence discipline requires.

transition_in.carries_over: What the two companies document.
transition_in.introduces: What neither of them publishes.

sections.heading: In Practice at Larkfield: Mila's €120, Party by Party
sections.controlling_idea: Followed party by party, Mila's €120 is approved by her bank at 19:42 on Tuesday, stays in her account that evening, reaches Studio Noord as €117.47 on Thursday and remains open to a dispute until early July.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the parties and the six steps to one payment with dates and amounts, and answers the scene's four questions.

flow.rationale: The cast first, then the payment in time order, then the answer to Wednesday's question, then the same payment on the other provider. The Stripe variant comes last because it changes only two cells of a table the reader has to have seen.

transition_in.carries_over: The parties, the timeline and the two providers' documented roles.
transition_in.introduces: All three applied to the one payment the book follows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every party in the model has a name in Mila's payment, and the one that needs care is the acquirer.

evidence.what: Role / who it is in Mila's payment / what it does here. Rows: cardholder (Mila Janssen), wallet (her phone's), issuer (her Dutch bank), network (Visa), acquirer and provider (Adyen; that Adyen N.V. is the acquirer of record is the author's inference from its license page, since Adyen publishes no complete list of acquiring entities per country), merchant (Studio Noord), platform (Larkfield).
evidence.shows: The abstract model maps onto the running example without remainder.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In time order the €120 is promised on Tuesday evening, claimed at once, moved between the banks over the next days, paid to the studio as €117.47 on Thursday 11 March and open to a dispute until about 7 July 2027.

evidence.what: When / step / who acts / where the €120 is. Rows: Tue 9 March 19:42 authorization and automatic capture; clearing and settlement on the following days (timing an assumption, industry practice); Thu 11 March payout of €117.47 after Larkfield's fee of €2.53; 120 calendar days from 9 March ends 7 July 2027 (the author's arithmetic on Visa's rule, which counts from the transaction processing date).
evidence.shows: Dates and amounts for each of the six steps, and the location of the money at each.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2015/751, Article 3: interchange on a consumer debit card transaction is capped at 0.2% of its value, at most €0.24 on €120.
evidence.shows: What the issuer keeps back is small and capped; the breakdown belongs to the economics chapter.

transition_in.carries_over: The cast.
transition_in.introduces: What each of them does, in order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At noon on Wednesday the honest answer to Ines is that the issuer has promised and the studio has claimed, the banks may or may not have settled, the payout comes tomorrow, and the payment stays reversible into July, so 'paid' was true and not final.

evidence.what: The four questions from the scene answered from the table: who approved (Mila's bank), has money moved (not to the studio), when does the studio receive it (Thursday), until when can it come back (about 7 July 2027). Keel decision K2 as the consequence for the payment record.
evidence.shows: Closes the scene and shows the can-do outcome on the book's own payment.

transition_in.carries_over: The dated walkthrough.
transition_in.introduces: The answer to the question the scene asked.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Had Studio Noord been on Stripe, the parties and the six steps would be the same and two cells would change: the acquirer would be the entity Stripe names for the EEA, and the payout would follow Stripe's clock.

evidence.what: Stripe acquirer disclosure: for the European Economic Area the "Payment Method Acquirer is Stripe Technology Europe, Ltd."; Stripe payouts page, country table: Netherlands, initial settlement timing 7 calendar days, default 3 business days.
evidence.shows: The differences between the providers on this payment are a named entity and a payout clock, not the model.
evidence.source: Stripe, Acquirer Disclosure & Acquirer Terms, https://stripe.com/en-us/legal/acquirer-disclosure, n.d., accessed 2026-11

transition_in.carries_over: The payment on Adyen.
transition_in.introduces: The same payment on Stripe.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Each Step Fails in Its Own Way
sections.controlling_idea: Because each step has its own owner and clock, each fails separately, and most payment incidents are a system treating one party's report as another party's fact.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of reading the provider's answer as the outcome: every Larkfield incident on the payment's path sits at a hand-off between two parties.

flow.rationale: The failures step by step with the incident each produced, then the rule that covers all of them; the rule would be an assertion without the table before it.

transition_in.carries_over: A chain of six steps that worked.
transition_in.introduces: What each step looks like when it does not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the six steps has a characteristic failure, a party that knows about it first and a chapter that treats it.

evidence.what: Step / what goes wrong / who knows first / Larkfield's case / chapter. Rows: authorization (no answer comes back: the Double Charge, 1 November 2026, 1,840 members charged twice, €71,300 refunded); capture (the approval expires before the claim); clearing and settlement (records disagree for days: the Unexplained €0.4 Million, €412,000); payout (returned by the receiving bank: the Payout That Bounced, 412 payouts, €386,000); dispute (arrives after payout: Bram de Wit's €120, 24 February 2027, €15.00 fee); the report of any step (the Silent Webhook, 14 September 2026, 9 hours, 3,200 memberships).
evidence.shows: The incidents the book returns to are spread along the timeline, one per hand-off.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rule that covers all six is to treat a missing or surprising answer as unknown, ask the party that owns the fact through the provider's own record, and keep looking until every payment has reached a state that party has confirmed.

evidence.what: The Phantom Payment pattern (a system believes a payment succeeded or failed without the provider's confirmed record) generalizes the table; Keel K2 (the provider's record is the truth, the webhook is the doorbell; a job sweeps everything pending) is Larkfield's version of the rule.
evidence.shows: Detection and recovery in one rule, with pointers to the chapters that own the mechanisms.

transition_in.carries_over: Six separate failures.
transition_in.introduces: The one rule of detection and recovery they share.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The parties, the timeline and the provider's position are one fact seen three ways: for every step of a payment there is a party that owns it, and the provider is the owner of only one, the payout. A status is therefore always somebody else's promise relayed, and the acquirer of record is the name of the party on whom most of those promises land first.
conclusion.so_what: An integrator who accepts this stops storing one status per payment, records which promise it holds and from whom, and puts one question to every provider in every country before any other: which legal entity is the acquirer.

callback.to: The opening minute after 19:42, when the app said the payment had succeeded and the €120 was still in Mila's account.
callback.how: The reader can now say who had decided what at 19:43, where the money was, and that the last open promise on that payment closes in July.

takeaway.content: For every status your system stores, write down whose decision it reports and what is still open after it; for every provider and country, write down the acquirer of record.

hand_off.carries_over: The six-step timeline and its parties, with authorization named as the first step and the only one the customer sees.
hand_off.introduces: What that first step contains: the message, the issuer's decision and codes, the hold and its expiry, and the case where no answer comes back.

transition_in.carries_over: The failures at each hand-off and the rule that covers them.
transition_in.introduces: What holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: the four-party structure and the three network services are the networks' own description, settlement is daily and net between members, the network does not guarantee the merchant's payout, and the dispute right runs for about 120 days.
Depends on context: which entity is the acquirer, when the payout arrives, and whether the payment can be disputed at all depend on the provider, the country and the payment method.

transition_in.carries_over: What the field agrees on.
transition_in.introduces: What changes with provider, country and method.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: treat every provider status as a relayed promise with an owner and an expiry, and ask for the acquirer of record before comparing providers on anything else.

transition_in.carries_over: What is established and what depends on context.
transition_in.introduces: The author's own position, labeled as such.
